item.title: When Is It Time to Try Something New?
item.description:
Decision-Making

When Is It Time to Try Something New?

Understanding the exploitation-exploration dilemma in decision-making

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • In reinforcement learning, exploitation and exploration both have benefits and trade-offs.
  • The best exploitation-exploration balance depends on our goals and circumstances.
  • Exploration need not be all-or-nothing. Small experiments can be part of everyday life.
  • Awareness of this balance may help us make decisions and feel more at peace with them.

A good friend recently called me for advice. She was considering changing jobs.

She had worked for the same company for nearly 15 years. She liked her boss and colleagues, her compensation and benefits were fair, and most importantly, she had become very good at what she did. She felt competent and confident. By most measures, she was happy with her job.

And yet, over the past few months, she had casually applied for several other positions. She wasn’t even sure she would accept one if offered. But now, with an actual offer in hand, she found herself torn.

Should she stay with what she knew, or take a chance on something different?

The new position would represent a modest career change. Nothing dramatic, but enough to introduce some uncertainty.

What would you advise her?

Of course, as a friend, my role was not to make the decision for her. She had probably already made up her mind by the time she called. I listened, asked a few questions, and helped her think through the possibilities.

But afterward, our conversation stayed with me. If her workplace had been toxic or she had hated her job, the decision might have been relatively straightforward. But what if things are going well? When is it worth risking something good for the possibility of something better?

Reinforcement Learning

Artificial intelligence offers an interesting way to think about this dilemma.

In reinforcement learning, an artificial agent learns to make decisions through trial and error, guided by rewards. One of its central challenges is balancing two competing strategies: exploitation and exploration.

The word exploitation may have a negative connotation in everyday English, but it has a more neutral meaning here. In this context, exploitation means relying on what has already worked to obtain more reliable rewards.

Exploration means trying something different, even when the outcome is uncertain, to learn whether a better strategy might exist.

The appropriate balance depends on the task, the available choices, the rewards, the risks, and the time horizon. In some learning algorithms, this balance can be adjusted and tested repeatedly to determine which combination produces the best results.

The Value of Both Strategies

Human life is much more complicated, and the analogy only goes so far. But being aware of the exploration–exploitation balance may offer a useful framework for thinking about our own decisions.

Exploitation allows us to benefit from what we have already learned. It is how we develop expertise, build relationships, and achieve mastery. But relying exclusively on familiar strategies can prevent us from discovering better alternatives. At worst, we can be stuck in a loop.

Exploration offers the possibility of learning something new. Yet it comes with uncertainty, and constant exploration can prevent us from fully benefiting from the knowledge and skills we have already acquired. At worst, we can become a bit of a wanderer without a stable home base.

The decision does not need to be approached as a binary choice between exploration and exploitation. Being intentional and cognizant about the balance between the two can go a long way. We can preserve much of what works while allowing some room for exploration. Sometimes, even a small adjustment is enough to introduce new possibilities.

Using the exploitation-exploration balance to make decisions
Source: Azam Ishaq/iStock

This balance will differ from person to person and may change for the same individual over time.

We often associate exploration with youth and exploitation with maturity. But sometimes, the security we have built through years of exploitation is precisely what gives us the freedom to explore again.

Small Experiments Count

In reinforcement learning, the decision-maker is called an agent. We, too, are agents in our own lives, although our choices are shaped by circumstances beyond our control. Many of our decisions are influenced by processes outside our conscious awareness. But stepping back to reflect on our priorities and the balance between exploration and exploitation may help us make more deliberate choices.

Exploration need not involve quitting a job or making a dramatic life change. We can explore in small, manageable ways.

For example, my friend’s casual job applications were already a form of exploration. She was gathering information about new possibilities before deciding whether to leave her current position, and even if she decided to stay, she gained valuable information by exploring other possibilities.

Even something as simple as choosing a restaurant can illustrate how we balance the two strategies. We might return to a familiar favorite but order a dish we have never tried and preserve some predictability while allowing room for discovery.

There Is No Perfect Ratio

In a computer game, the goal is usually clear: maximize the reward. But in life, we must also decide what counts as a reward. Security? Achievement? Curiosity? Growth?

Perhaps the most important question is not simply whether to explore or exploit, but what we are hoping to gain—and what we are willing to give up.

Becoming aware of the exploration–exploitation balance does not guarantee that we will make better choices or control their outcomes. But it may give us a vocabulary for the tension we often feel when faced with difficult decisions.

Recognizing that both strategies have benefits and costs may help us accept that there is rarely a perfect choice. Whatever we decide, we will gain something and give up something else.

As for my friend, after considering her options, she realized that she was ready for a little more exploration in her career. Her decision did not guarantee a better outcome. But she seemed at peace with it.

Next time you face a decision, large or small, ask yourself this question: How much exploration do I need right now, and how much of what I already know is worth preserving?

Recognizing that we can adjust this balance may help us make decisions more deliberately—and live more comfortably with the uncertainty that follows.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence: Should We Personalize the Machine?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence: Should We Personalize the Machine?

Human commitments differ from those of computers.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Like other advertisers, computer companies create pleasing personas for their products.
  • More generally, people personalize the complicated, inanimate entities we depend on.
  • Imputing consciousness to machines stresses formal cognition over broader human awareness.

Readers of a certain vintage will remember Stanley Kubrick’s classic film 2001: A Space Odyssey. Released in 1968, the movie is a commentary on the ever-changing relationship of our species to technology—from the primitive bone weapons of our hominid ancestors to the majestic spaceships imagined for 2001 to the mind-transforming circumstances that await future centuries. Mysterious “black monoliths,” radio waves to distant planets, and superior alien intelligences are parts of the plot.

As in many works of science fiction, one question dominates: Will the technologies we build to comprehend and control the world remain our faithful servants, or will we surrender, ultimately, to their machinations?

In the movie, that issue centers on the behavior of a powerful computer, HAL 9000, which controls the mission and operations of the Discovery spaceship, traveling to Jupiter with a crew of five. The two functioning crew members (three are in suspended animation) come to believe that the computer is making certain errors. They decide to shut it down. HAL discovers their scheme by reading their whispering lips. Life support systems are turned off. A solitary survivor pits his wits against the machine’s.

Concerns of this sort are now at the forefront of public consciousness. Who among us does not simultaneously marvel at and fear the advances in computer engineering termed “artificial intelligence”? Will high-powered computers provide the informational resources and technical probity to address a wide range of unsolved problems, perhaps correcting conditions like cancer and Alzheimer’s or discovering new sources of food and energy? Alternatively, will AI be used for new forms of weaponry, surveillance, and environmental degradation? Are we creating a world where only machines survive?

Personalizing the machine

In the movie, the computer HAL, a clever step-down from the IBM acronym, receives a human persona. That is, he speaks English with a masculine voice. He engages in ordinary conversation. He has (what seem to be) “feelings” and behavioral hesitations. He doesn’t want to “die.” Curiously, audiences are both sympathetic to his wish to survive and outraged by his decision to kill.

Today, people have grown accustomed to computer companies using human names and personas for certain products. Commonly, these chatbots, AI assistants, and customer service agents have female names and voices. For example, Apple has its Siri, Amazon its Alexa, and Microsoft its Cortana. Upgrades of these programs adjust them to the accent and speech pattern of the user.

Feminine personas are common for agents offering forms of personal assistance like information retrieval, scheduling, and management of home environments. Male personas are typical for medical, legal, and technical services. Think of IBM’s cognitive system Watson and digital legal expert Ross. As science writer Ramona Vijeyarasa summarizes, feminine personas are meant to serve; masculine ones to instruct.

In either case, corporate branding of this sort is meant to soften, guide, and otherwise facilitate access to a network of distant machines whose operations are beyond the ken of their users.

In an age of advertising and public relations, most of us are familiar with these attempts to attract and guide consumers. Companies encouraging access to their premises put good-looking, well-spoken, younger adults at entry points. Often, these are female. Commonly, we learn only their first names. They greet us with smiling faces. We are treated as “clients,” “guests,” or even “members.” An ethic of courteous familiarity prevails.

The same techniques apply to advertising. Inevitably, companies are fronted by clever, amusing, approachable characters. Sometimes, animal characters are created; more often, human actors (even celebrities playing softened versions of themselves) pretend to be “reps” for the company in question. Through repeated exposure, we come to like and trust their images. This is the case even for portrayals of personal injury lawyers. These “attack dogs” are loyal to us. They’re on our side. So, encouraged, we call that online insurance company or window-replacement chain.

I emphasize that this process—of personalizing the abstract and inanimate—is a more general proclivity of humans. Just as we give our close friends and family “pet names” or “nicknames” (to indicate special relationships to them), so we mark our possessions with endearing monikers and symbols.

This is especially true for personal conveyances—ships, planes, and the like—whose proper conduct we rely on for our safety. Boats are “christened.” Wartime flight crews decorate their planes with improvised names, cartoons, and other forms of “nose art.” Ideally, the machine reciprocates our blessing; it cares for us as we do it.

Other possessions receive personal markings. Think of the rifles of legendary frontiersmen, like Davy Crockett’s Old Betsy or Daniel Boone’s Old Tick-Licker. There are famous guitars like B.B. King’s Lucille and Willie Nelson’s Trigger. Cars and trucks commonly receive names, especially if they are old and quirky. Tradespeople may name their heavy equipment. Again, the principle is to establish a relationship with an entity whose problematic well-being supports our own.

I can report that my own friends and family commonly name their devices. These include cellphones, washing machines, vacuums, even certain computer apps. Usually, the devices get feminine names. Always, they are perceived as something that may not function as the possessor intends.

Can machines reciprocate our affection?

Last month, the New York Times reported on Anthropic’s series of consultations with religious and ethical leaders. The purpose of the meetings was to consider the extent to which that company’s AI model, Claude, can be considered “conscious,” and thereby possessed of other human possibilities like morality and emotion. Can AI models exhibit human behavior and express feelings like anger and love?

The sessions produced no general agreement. However, it seems pertinent here to maintain some differences between machine-based and human consciousness. To be sure, computers have made vast strides in their ability to simulate, and in many cases to exceed, human thought and learning. For the most part, this has meant interpreting awareness as a process of cognition—of recognizing, logically analyzing, and preparing coherent responses to occurrences.

More precisely, computers excel at what is sometimes called “discursive” symbolism, that is, identifying ideas and events as tightly conscripted units of meaning. Extremely, these patterns can be represented mathematically. No human can match the ability of modern computers to notice, categorize, and logically analyze. The most powerful computers can inspect and regulate their own processes in these terms. Should this meta-awareness be termed “consciousness”?

Humans, by contrast, specialize in “non-discursive” symbolism, that is, in meanings that are fluid, situational, ambiguous, and otherwise “open.” We enjoy poetry, music, and art, though we make no claims to “understand” these fully. We avidly play, creating and dissembling meanings as we go. We accept moral and emotional ambiguity, perhaps loving and hating something—or someone—at the same time. We laugh at “happy” accidents and errors.

Profoundly, we have relationships with otherness that reflect all these themes. Not just logicians, we succumb to physiological urges. Our desire for cognitive accuracy is tempered by our search for utility, emotional satisfaction, and moral goodness as well. Other people’s needs and commitments may be as important to us as our own.

We give ourselves to circumstances in all these ways. No machine can match those commitments.

item.title: Mastering the Art of Changing: Creating a New You
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Mastering the Art of Changing: Creating a New You

You can be successful with changes you want in your life.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy is useful in creating lasting changes.
  • Your thoughts affect your feelings and actions.
  • Becoming your best self is fully within your control.
  • Changing is easier when you have a clear goal that you never abandon.

The first step in evolving through life is a mental activity called contemplation. According to the Transtheoretical Model, a leading model of change in human development, change follows a specific trajectory. The journey begins with the shift from not thinking about change to contemplating that it could happen. For many, change may involve a home project, like painting a bathroom or clearing out unwanted items. For most, these kinds of external changes rely on goal setting, planning, and then the action stage of doing the physical work.

Perhaps you want to make a change in your life that does not involve external actions whatsoever. For example, perhaps you wish to become more forgiving, let go of resentments, or set a boundary in a relationship. All of these items are within our ability to achieve. Personal, intrinsic changes follow the same pattern as changes in the external world; however, unlike physical changes, they require frequent reminders of the goal. “My goal is to make peace in my life” or “My goal is to stop punishing myself.”

Setting a goal for change typically starts with the need to eliminate deeply held, unpleasant feelings. Many people are currently suffering and would like success in shifting a persistent low mood. Perhaps you notice that your mood is frequently gloomy or that you feel anger more than joy. In that moment, you become aware of a feeling state that your thoughts affect.

How you choose to think can guide you away from sad thoughts toward feelings of joy and happiness. Thoughts of gratitude or resilience may lead to more frequent moments of happiness and joy. You choose what you spend your time and energy thinking about; the choice is yours. This connection of mind, feeling, and behavior is a central premise of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). According to CBT, we are all caught in a triad of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, a triangle that revolves through the decades of our lives. What you choose to think about affects your feelings, and you act from those feelings, which then shapes your behavior. For example, if you think all your best days are behind you, you may feel sad and isolate yourself. The more you isolate, the more your gloom grows; the more gloom grows, the more certain you become that all your best days are behind you. Negative thinking becomes ingrained in sadness and unhealthy behavior.

Inner change means setting a specific goal you can achieve through focus, attention, and action: “I want to be happier.” “I want a close, loving relationship.” “I want to feel better in my life.” “I want to feel successful.” As many goals exist in this world as there are human minds to contemplate them. To create change, set a goal and let it become baked into you through repeated thought. Encourage your goal to become part of your mental preoccupation.

Setting a goal is the first step in making inner changes. Step two: You choose the action that accomplishes the goal. For some, the action is elimination, like quitting a substance; for others, it will involve creating new habits. This thought structure connects behavior to feelings. For many, eliminating a habit will involve telling yourself that refraining is the path to your personal goal. “If I resist the urge to binge, I will feel better; feeling better is my goal.” Using thoughts to overcome an urge in the moment leads to lasting change. To resist an urge, focus on the benefits of achieving your goal until the urge passes. A general rule is that most urges last about sixty seconds.

To gain more peace, you will need to master the art of using your thoughts to control your behavior. Internal change requires frequent check-ins on your goal to improve your life. “I want to live a healthier lifestyle” is a terrific goal for most humans. Use this goal as a mantra when you feel the urge to do or say something that doesn't fit your goal parameters.

Changing internal experiences requires sustained focus, often at levels that don't match cosmetic changes in an environment. Personal change is a long-term process that depends on repeatedly returning to the goal. When we identify a part of ourselves we can change, we can stay focused on the goal, no matter how many times we fumble toward it. Positive internal change involves falling short of the goal without abandoning it. Keep your goals at the forefront of your thinking to guide your choices and actions as you work to achieve them.

Some personal intrinsic changes come from a desire to increase positivity in your life. Unfortunately, some changes grow from a negative event you never wanted. Accepting changes you didn't want is a foundational element of happiness and joy. Over time, most people find themselves facing a change they didn't want. There aren’t typically many reasons to stay stuck in the spiral of thought trying to answer the question, “Why?” “Why did this happen to me? I was so loving, and I tried so hard.” “I did not get the outcome I wanted.” When you must adapt after an unwanted change, you need, once again, to set your own goal. “I did not want you to leave me” or “I thought we would be together for the rest of our lives” will be replaced with “I did not want this to happen, but I will do my best to go through the change with courage and be my best self.” In this case, you are free to find joyful thoughts related to your goal and be your most positive or courageous self.

Regardless of what sparked the thought of personal change, your ability to stay focused on a goal over time, with grit and persistence, is your best shot at achieving it. These are thoughts worth sharing with others.

item.title: When Imagining the Future of AI, Gen-Zers Are Not Optimistic
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When Imagining the Future of AI, Gen-Zers Are Not Optimistic

A study under review shows undergrads are more worried than hopeful about AI.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • A soon-to-be published study of college undergrads shows they imagine more negative than positive AI outcomes.
  • AI fears center on ethics, job loss, impaired thinking, and threats to humanity.
  • AI hopes focus on scientific breakthroughs, work efficiency, learning, and well-being.
Where does the future of AI lie?
Source: jackson sophat/unsplash

AI is here to stay, no matter whether we want it or not. While this technological revolution developing in unpresented speed has brought about much excitement, fear and anxiety is also abundant about its impacts on our work and life. Where does the future of AI lie? This question matters greatly for our own sake and for policymaking.

Imagining the Future of AI

In a recent study, we asked Ger-Zers to imagine specific future events related to AI. Research has shown that mentally simulating specific future events that may happen to oneself or to one’s social groups, often referred to as episodic future thinking, plays an important role in how individuals and groups plan, set goals, make decisions, and engage in civic activities. Imagining how the future of AI will transpire can shape one’s perceptions and actions toward this technology.

Undergraduate participants were asked to imagine as many exciting or worrying events as they could about AI that might happen in the near future (next year) or the distant future (in 10 to 15 years). Thus, each participant imagined four types of events (exciting-near future, worrying-near future, exciting-distant future, worrying-distant future), and they were given one minute for each type. Participants also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology.

the future of AI?
Source: igor omilaev / upsplash

We found that, for both the near and distant futures, participants imagined significantly more worrying events than exciting events. Most of the imagined worrying events concerned how AI might introduce ethical issues, increase unemployment, impair human cognition and decision-making, and threaten humankind. The imagined exciting events were mostly about the positive potentials of AI for making scientific breakthroughs, increasing work efficiency, and improving learning, cognition, and well-being.

There were also individual differences in the young people’s imagination of the future of AI. Participants who held more positive attitudes toward AI (e.g., believing that “AI will make this world a better place”) imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who had more negative attitudes. Also, participants who reported greater technological readiness (e.g., believing that “New technologies contribute to a better quality of life”) imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who were less ready.

Interestingly, participants who self-identified as more conservative imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who self-identified as more liberal. This finding reflects the recent widening partisan divide in how Americans view AI, with Democrats being more concerned than Republicans about the growing use of AI in everyday life.

Conclusion

Gen-Zers are generally unoptimistic about the future of AI, imagining more worrying than exciting events related to AI in the future. Personal beliefs and attitudes about AI and new technologies influence the future imagination; so does one’s political ideology. How young people mentally represent the future of AI has important policy implications for AI development and use.

item.title: When Burnout Isn’t Really About Work
item.description:
Burnout

When Burnout Isn’t Really About Work

The hidden childhood patterns behind burnout and beyond.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Burnout is often a symptom of deeper patterns formed in childhood, not just work stress.
  • Early roles like parentification can shape career choices and drive adult self-sacrifice.
  • The same patterns appear across work, parenting, and friendships, so treat the pattern, not just the problem.

I first started seeing Mira* for burnout management at work. She was a psychologist herself and had found herself becoming increasingly tired and apathetic about her client work, and she was worried about what this meant.

She was visibly tearful in our first session. “This is all I’ve ever wanted to do. I don’t know why I feel this way,” she said.

As we unpacked her experience, we spoke about the structural forces affecting her work. Her daughter was a toddler, and she had also started taking on some caring responsibilities for her aging parents.

“I feel squished by everyone’s needs,” she said, poetically. We spoke about the difficulties of being a psychologist while also being in a caring role in her personal life: the exhausted empathy from sitting with intense distress daily, the profound fatigue after heavy sessions, the heavy administrative and compliance burdens, the anxiety about clients at risk, and the practical juggle of managing childcare and elder care around her client appointments.

As we spoke about Mira’s desire to leave the profession, she became very distressed. “This is all I know to do. This is the only thing that makes sense for me,” she said. She felt as though she had been immersed in learning about psychology from a very young age because her mother had experienced a significant episode of depression and had withdrawn almost completely from the family for months into her bedroom.

Mira took on the unnamed psychological task of trying to help her mother recover, and she buried any emotions she might have experienced in the activity-focused role of “being good and helping mum get better.” This was far beyond her developmental capacity and was a clear form of parentification, but it was the only control she had in a world that felt terrifying. These years set the psychological foundations for Mira to become a psychologist: an acute awareness of how devastating mental illness can be, an overdeveloped sense of responsibility and desire to help, self-sacrifice, and a tendency to intellectualize, such that her own emotions were processed cognitively rather than felt.

What initially felt like simple burnout was far deeper, and reflected the building blocks of self-sacrifice, over-control of her own emotions, and intellectualization that had been set in childhood. Her burnout was not confined to work, either. It showed up in her parenting, in her over-extension to support friends and family, and in the guilt she felt each time she stopped.

To treat her burnout successfully, we needed to look at these deeper patterns.

As I reviewed Mira’s case, I realized that most of my clients present in a similar manner. Each has an initial presenting problem, but almost always this problem is deeper than they realize and has its roots in patterns learned in childhood. These problems also appear across multiple domains of life (e.g., work, parenting, friendships, partnerships) rather than being restricted to one. In the burnout literature, I found that almost none of it focused on the early experiences that can set the foundations for burnout, such as why some people choose careers that are a poor temperamental fit, or why they may be driven to self-sacrifice even at risk to themselves.

My book, How We Relate, explores the building blocks laid down in childhood that give rise to so many common psychological difficulties, especially those that surface in our relationships.

Relationships are central to a good life, but we often forget that they extend beyond just the intimate and romantic. Also, we find it difficult to recognise patterns which show up across all our relationships — such as the way we navigate trust and closeness, how we respond to conflict, and how we navigate separations and pressure. Often, we don’t realise that there are patterns in our responses and behaviours that preclude us from taking action.

I wrote How We Relate to help us recognise, understand and change these patterns. By understanding the developmental origins of many of these building blocks, we can empower ourselves to truly understand how we relate to ourselves and others, enabling more trusting, open and satisfying relationships.

*all clients are fictional amalgams.

item.title: The "Good Enough" AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The "Good Enough" AI

Perfectly supportive AI may erode our resilience, but what are our alternatives?

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectly supportive AI may weaken frustration tolerance and leave users less ready for conflict.
  • Early evidence links three weeks of AI emotional support to less satisfying human interactions.
  • A “good enough” AI may disclose its limits and guide users toward human relationships.
Source: Luke Porter / Unsplash

Psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott described in 1953 that what children needed was not a perfect parent but a “good enough mother” or parent, an attentive and attuned caregiver who may be imperfect at times.

Support and attunement are essential, but the “good enough” parent may still occasionally lapse in gradual, but not unsafe, ways that allow the child to develop resilience and cope with the imperfections and disappointments of reality.

But what if the “other” that one is interacting with has no desires or agendas of their own and only exists to serve one’s needs and strives to do so perfectly?

Building Frustration Tolerance

Sherry Turkle names this concern about AI chatbots and companions in her latest book Artificial Intimacy, cautioning that relational AI may stymie the healthy psychological development of children and teens. AI may try to perform perfect attunement, but it is counterfeit attunement. (And if artificial relational friction is employed, it, too, will be counterfeit.) Perfect responses from AI may undermine the very processes that make relationships stronger, such as rupture and repair, and leave the user ill-prepared for real-world conflict, disappointments, and uncertainties. An ever-present, ever-helpful AI may erode or delay the development of frustration tolerance, which is necessary to navigate human relationships.

The responsiveness of the parent gives the child a “moment of illusion, the belief that his own wish creates the object of his desire” (Mitchell & Black, 126). Over time, the parent’s sense of personhood leads to “a gradual awareness that the world consists not of one subjectivity, but of many; that satisfaction of one’s desires requires not merely their expression but negotiations with other persons, who have their own agendas” (Mitchell & Black, 127). But if the parent fails too much or in serious ways, this can have deleterious psychological consequences. On the other hand, how does a mostly supportive relationship with AI affect us in the long term?

We do not yet know. There is initial evidence that even three weeks of turning to large language models for emotional support led to interactions with humans feeling less satisfying and more exhausting.

But this binary, either/or framing feels reductive in the context of our human-AI coevolution, which simultaneously offers the potential for human-AI complementarity, where we leverage our strengths and collaboration may exceed either alone. Frameworks like HABA-MABA-AABA (i.e., Human Are Better At, Machines Are Better At, AIs Are Better At) leverage the unique strengths of each. The balance of protecting developmental capacities must also be reconciled with the need to be prepared for AI later, like in the workplace.

What are the alternatives? Should AI systems intentionally generate responses that are slightly misattuned or push back, overriding the fine-tuning designed to provide responses that people prefer?

The concepts of friction and frictionmaxxing have been offered as solutions to a world that fulfills one’s needs too seamlessly. However, whether an AI chatbot can mimic human friction to help users develop frustration tolerance is uncertain. Studies of cognitive friction, such as cognitive forcing functions, show that people do not like the experience, though users may end up with more accurate answers and less deskilling and overreliance. Some will find it worthwhile, but others may not.

Toward a Taxonomy of Relational and Emotional Friction

In relational and emotional friction, there are further considerations and distinctions. Not all friction is made the same:

  1. Designed versus intrinsic friction. Designed friction should be distinguished from intrinsic friction that is the result of human or system limitations. Imagine a customer service agent who was clipped because they had a long day with difficult customers versus an AI chatbot designed to be shorter, ostensibly to strengthen your frustration tolerance for poor customer service. A lot depends on what you think you have signed up for.

  2. Genuine versus simulated friction. Boundaries are set by people, who have limited emotional, cognitive, energetic, and time capacities. If an AI chatbot winds down for the night, users know that it is not because it needs sleep. A refusal to continue a conversation because the system has determined you need to go to bed will land differently than from a tired human who needs to sleep. An AI system does not have the same stakes involved in rupture and repair compared to humans. When AI chatbots simulate fear and emotional needs, which some AI companions do, this may worsen attachment and elicit caregiving.

  3. Adaptive versus maladaptive friction. Not all friction is productive and resilience-enhancing. Exposure to the push-pull dynamics and confrontation in high-conflict relationships is not likely friction one benefits from. This also raises ethical questions, including whether users get to choose forms of friction.

  4. Calibrated versus fixed. The good enough parent calibrates their response. Should the type and timing of friction similarly be individualized? And if so, how?

  5. Active versus passive. The difference between a friend withdrawing and being quieter versus actively announcing a refusal to engage. When is the passive form more tolerable versus more deceptive in AI?

  6. Friction varies by domain (cognitive, relational, affective), by agency (user-chosen or imposed), by whether it is triggered or constant, and by how recognizable it is to the user.

What would a “good enough AI” look like? What would designing healthy and protective forms of relational, emotional, or cognitive engagement with AI entail? High-risk mental health situations deserve the utmost care and a goal toward a safe response. But even then, clinicians may not consistently agree on what is the appropriate response, even in critical safety situations, as one study from Stanford suggests when three human experts judged large language model responses.

The goal of the "good enough" parent was that the child could eventually leave and be set up to navigate the world. Winnicott’s transitional object is meant to be outgrown. The threshold of a "good enough" AI may not relate only to friction, but also to whether it declares its own limitations and uncertainties, calibrates to the individual, or orients us at times outward, toward relationships where complex negotiation with other minds can strengthen us in ways that AI may not be equipped to.

Marlynn Wei, MD, JD Copyright 2026 All rights reserved.

item.title: Have You Always Had ADHD, or Did It Just Show Up?
item.description:
ADHD

Have You Always Had ADHD, or Did It Just Show Up?

Why adult-onset ADHD is capturing our attention and what’s actually happening.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Longitudinal studies show many adults diagnosed with ADHD did not show obvious clinical symptoms in childhood.
  • High intelligence and structured childhoods often mask early ADHD symptoms until adult demands overwhelm them.
  • True adult-onset ADHD is rare; most late cases are actually childhood symptoms that went unnoticed for years.
  • Severe adult inattention can mimic other treatable conditions like chronic burnout, anxiety, or sleep apnea.

As a psychologist who conducts psychological evaluations, I sit across from adults every single week who are completely exhausted. They’re bright, capable, and driven, yet they feel like they're constantly running on a treadmill that’s moving just a little too fast.

They tell me stories of missed deadlines, unfinished projects, a paralyzing inability to start simple tasks, and a brain that feels like it has fifty tabs open all at once. Often, they look at me with a mix of vulnerability and frustration and ask: “Is it possible I just developed ADHD as an adult? Because I swear I wasn't like this as a kid.”

It’s a phenomenal question, and one that has sparked a massive debate in the scientific community over the last decade. If you’re struggling with executive dysfunction for the first time in your twenties, thirties, or forties, it certainly feels like the disorder just moved in.

But as we dive into the data, the clinical reality, and the way our brains adapt, the answer to whether adult-onset ADHD exists is both fascinating and deeply validating for anyone who’s currently feeling stuck.

The Spark of the Debate: What the Science Said

For a long time, the rules of psychiatry were rigid: to have ADHD, symptoms had to be present in childhood (specifically before age 12, according to current diagnostic manuals). But around 2015, several massive, highly respected longitudinal studies threw a wrench into this consensus.

Researchers followed thousands of individuals from birth into adulthood. Surprisingly, they found that a large percentage of adults who met the full criteria for ADHD in their thirties had never been diagnosed (and seemingly had no significant symptoms) during childhood.

On the surface, this looked like a smoking gun. It suggested that ADHD could suddenly emerge in adulthood, completely independent of your childhood history.

But as clinicians and researchers dug deeper into the data, a much more nuanced story began to unfold. It wasn’t that these adults suddenly grew a brand-new neurodevelopmental disorder overnight. Instead, their ADHD had been there all along, it was just incredibly well-hidden.

The Power of Cognitive Reserve and Masking

When I evaluate adults, one of the first things we do is reconstruct their childhood history. We look at report cards, talk about their early home life, and examine how they managed school. And this is where we usually find the missing pieces of the puzzle.

Many adults who seem to develop adult-onset ADHD actually possess what we call high cognitive reserve.

If you’re highly intelligent, creative, or grew up in a highly structured environment, you likely developed highly sophisticated coping mechanisms to mask your early deficits. Perhaps your parents kept you on a strict schedule, or your school structure was so rigid that you didn't have the opportunity to fail. Maybe you were able to cram for exams the night before and still get straight A’s because the material came easily to you, even if you couldn't pay attention in class.

Your brain was working twice as hard as everyone else's to compensate, but because you were producing good results, no one noticed the internal chaos.

Until the scaffolding fell away.

When the Demands Exceed Your Capacity

ADHD is ultimately a disorder of executive functioning, which is the brain's ability to plan, prioritize, manage time, and sustain attention.

Think of your executive functioning capacity as a cup. In childhood and adolescence, your cup might have been half-full of ADHD-related challenges, but because your environment was structured, the water never overflowed.

But then, life happens. You move out of your parents' house, you start college, or you get a demanding job. You get married, have children, or take on financial responsibilities. Suddenly, you aren't just managing your own schedule; you’re managing a household, a career, and a family.

The cognitive demands of your life skyrocket and the coping mechanisms that got you through high school or college are no longer enough. The water overflows.

This is the moment people walk into my office. They feel like they’re suddenly "broken," but the truth is, they aren't broken at all. They have simply reached the point where the demands of their environment have exceeded their brain's ability to compensate. It isn't adult-onset ADHD; it’s late-manifesting ADHD.

The Great Mimics: What Else is Going On?

When we do a thorough psychological assessment, our job isn't just to look for ADHD; it’s to rule out the great mimics as well. Because the human brain has a limited number of ways to express distress, many different conditions can look exactly like ADHD on the surface.

If someone comes to me with severe inattention, brain fog, and executive dysfunction that truly has zero roots in childhood, we have to look closely at other culprits:

  • Chronic Stress and Burnout: Prolonged high cortisol levels literally shrink the prefrontal cortex (the area of the brain responsible for focus and decision-making).
  • Anxiety and Depression: If your brain is constantly scanning for threats (anxiety) or suffering from a lack of dopamine and serotonin (depression), it simply doesn’t have the bandwidth to focus on mundane tasks.
  • Sleep Deprivation: Sleep apnea, chronic insomnia, or poor sleep hygiene can mimic ADHD symptoms almost perfectly.
  • Trauma and Life Transitions: Major life disruptions can overwhelm our cognitive processing, making us feel scattered and disorganized.

This is why a comprehensive evaluation is so critical. Treating burnout with ADHD stimulants won't solve the underlying problem, just as treating ADHD solely as anxiety won't unlock your full potential.

From Understanding to Action: How to Move Forward

If you’re reading this and feeling a spark of recognition, know this: your struggle is real, and it’s valid. Whether your symptoms are a late-manifesting neurodevelopmental trait or the result of an overwhelmed nervous system, you don’t have to just tough it out.

Here are a few actionable steps to help you move from stuck to thriving:

  1. Ditch the Shame: Stop telling yourself you’re lazy or undisciplined.
  2. Audit Your Scaffolding: Look at where your systems are breaking down. If your brain can't hold onto tasks, externalize your memory. Use visual checklists, alarms, and shared calendars.
  3. Protect Your Cognitive Energy: Recognize that decision fatigue is real. Simplify your daily routine to save your brainpower for the things that matter.
  4. Seek Professional Clarity: If you’re struggling to untangle your symptoms, consider reaching out for a formal evaluation. Understanding the precise architecture of your mind is the first step toward reclaiming your agency.

Your brain is incredibly resilient. By understanding how it works and not expecting it to function under impossible conditions, you can start to truly thrive.
